name: The Bhutan Cypress of Burnley Gardens

location.address: Burnley Gardens, University of Melbourne Burnley campus, 500 Yarra Boulevard, Burnley VIC 3121

verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 163): dbh 103cm, height 13m, significance 'Rare or Localised, Particularly Old', surveyed 2012-10-04

Burnley Gardens (University of Melbourne Faculty of Science) confirmed as a nine-hectare public garden of nearly 1,000 plant species including some of the city's oldest trees; multiple independent descriptions (science.unimelb.edu.au, tripadvisor.com.au, gardendrum.com) corroborate the garden's identity and heritage-tree collection, but none names this individual Cupressus torulosa by species. Single-source on species/age for this specific tree.
access: Free, open to the public. Grounds of the University of Melbourne's Burnley campus (Burnley Gardens), a public botanic garden with no gate charge.
transport: Burnley railway station (Glen Waverley/Alamein/Belgrave/Lilydale lines) is roughly a 10 minute walk; tram route 78 runs along Swan Street nearby.
verify_notes: Only the City of Yarra register names this tree; no second independent source located for THIS individual despite searching Friends of Burnley Gardens (page currently 404s), two Gardendrum long-reads on Burnley's historic trees, the Garden History Society's Burnley PDF (scanned, no extractable text), and iNaturalist (nearest Cupressus torulosa observation found was ~750m away, casual grade, not a match). Flag is for single-sourcing, not for doubt about existence: Burnley Gardens is a well-documented, actively managed heritage garden and conifers of this kind are exactly what such registers exist to record. dbh 103cm converts to a girth of about 3.24 metres (circumference = diameter x pi); the register measures across the trunk, not around it. Height 13m is modest for the species' potential (Cupressus torulosa can exceed 30m in its native Himalayan range), consistent with a tree grown in cultivation rather than forest conditions. Joins the Burnley Gardens cluster with mel_010/011/012 below, about 450-600m from mel_007 (Osage Orange, Yarra Boulevard) and forms the western end of a walk that runs Burnley Gardens to Yarra Bend Park.

name: The River Red Gum of Burnley Gardens

location.address: Burnley Gardens, University of Melbourne Burnley campus, 500 Yarra Boulevard, Burnley VIC 3121

verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 228): dbh 92cm, height 17m, significance 'Significant Habitat Value, Outstanding Size, Remnant, Particularly Old', surveyed 2012-10-04

Gardendrum, 'Burnley's Secret Botanic Garden Part 3' (gardendrum.com/2015/07/11): describes a River Red Gum in the southwest corner of Burnley Gardens' Native Garden believed to exceed 400 years old and to pre-date European colonisation of the site. Corroborates species, remnant status and general location (Native Garden, Burnley Gardens) but does NOT confirm this is the same individual tree as register ref 228; treat as a plausible but unconfirmed match, not proof.

iNaturalist: Eucalyptus camaldulensis observations within the Burnley campus grounds as recently as 2025-05-20 (obs 282527453, ~380m away, needs_id) confirm the species is present and alive in the immediate area, though not pinned to this exact tree.
access: Free, open to the public. Grounds of the University of Melbourne's Burnley campus (Burnley Gardens), a public botanic garden with no gate charge.
transport: Burnley railway station (Glen Waverley/Alamein/Belgrave/Lilydale lines) is roughly a 10 minute walk; tram route 78 runs along Swan Street nearby.
verify_notes: SOURCES CONFLICT ON AGE, deliver both: the register's own band is the coarse 'over 100 years' used across this whole city page; Gardendrum's independent account of a Native Garden river red gum names a specific claim of 400+ years and pre-European remnant status, which would make it far older than anything else on the Melbourne page. I could not confirm the register's ref 228 IS the specific tree Gardendrum describes (Burnley Gardens' Native Garden may hold more than one old red gum, and the register gives no sub-location finer than the property address). Recommend the story state the register's conservative band as the figure and mention the unconfirmed 400-year local claim as a caveat rather than a fact, exactly as the published mel_002/mel_008 entries already do for the city's other 'remnant' red gums. dbh 92cm converts to a girth of about 2.89 metres (circumference = diameter x pi); register measures diameter, not the way round. Joins the Burnley Gardens cluster with mel_009/011/012, about 550m from mel_007 (Osage Orange) and roughly 1.0km from mel_008 (the other Yarra Boulevard River Red Gum), forming the western end of walk 2.

name: The Sugar Gum of Burnley Gardens

location.address: Burnley Gardens, University of Melbourne Burnley campus, 500 Yarra Boulevard, Burnley VIC 3121

verified_sources: City of Yarra Significant Trees register (data/registers/melbourne-yarra-significant-trees.json, ref 229): dbh 144cm, height 22m, significance 'Particularly Old, Outstanding Size, Location of Landscape Context', surveyed 2012-10-04

iNaturalist observation 313237418, research grade, 2025-09-12, Eucalyptus cladocalyx (sugar gum) at -37.82679,145.01689, i.e. within about 25 metres of this register point: confirms species and continued life at essentially this exact spot as of September 2025.
access: Free, open to the public. Grounds of the University of Melbourne's Burnley campus (Burnley Gardens), a public botanic garden with no gate charge.
transport: Burnley railway station (Glen Waverley/Alamein/Belgrave/Lilydale lines) is roughly a 10 minute walk; tram route 78 runs along Swan Street nearby.
verify_notes: IMPORTANT CHECK ALREADY DONE: Burnley Gardens' Heritage Victoria-listed Sugar Gum (a landmark at the entrance drive, dated c.1887) was removed in 2008 due to persistent limb drop, its timber later carved into the 'Sugar Gum Table' unveiled in 2013 (findanexpert.unimelb.edu.au / theconversation.com coverage of sugar gums, and Garden History Society material). This raised a real doubt that register ref 229 (surveyed 2012, after that removal) might be describing a dead tree. The doubt is resolved: a research-grade iNaturalist observation from September 2025, at coordinates essentially identical to ref 229 (within ~25m), independently confirms a living sugar gum at this spot, so this is either a second specimen from the removed entrance-drive tree or the same register point re-populated/never the same tree at all; either way there is direct recent evidence of a living Eucalyptus cladocalyx here. Flagged anyway because I cannot rule out this being a distinct, more recently established tree rather than the register's original 2012 specimen (dbh from a fresh planting would not reach 144cm by 2025, so the register's tree and the 2025 observation are very likely the same individual, but this is inference, not documentary proof). dbh 144cm converts to a girth of about 4.52 metres (circumference = diameter x pi); that is a heavy trunk but NOT the thickest on the page, still behind mel_001's holm oak (5.56m) and mel_003's elm (4.84m), so do not claim any girth superlative for this tree. Sugar gums are also documented locally as 'risky branch-droppers' (University of Melbourne research, 2024), worth a line on why old specimens are unusual to find still standing. Joins the Burnley Gardens cluster with mel_009/010/012, essentially the same spot as mel_010 (about 25m apart) and about 590m from mel_007.

No second source found; searched Wikipedia's Eucalyptus cornuta page (no Burnley mention), the two Gardendrum Burnley long-reads, Friends of Burnley Gardens (404s currently), and iNaturalist (zero E. cornuta observations found within 2km). Flag for single-sourcing rather than doubt: Yate is a genuinely unusual species to find this large outside Western Australia (its native range is the southwest WA coast), which is exactly the kind of 'Rare or Localised' specimen a university teaching garden collects, consistent with the register's own significance tags. dbh 127cm converts to a girth of about 3.99 metres (circumference = diameter x pi); register measures diameter, not the way round. This is the only entry on the whole Melbourne page whose age comes from a narrower register band (81-100 years, i.e. planted roughly 1926-1945) rather than the generic '100+ years' catch-all; say so plainly, it is a real distinction not an error. Joins the Burnley Gardens cluster with mel_009/010/011, about 30m from mel_011 (Sugar Gum) and 570m from mel_007.
